title-group.article-title: Effectiveness of linvoseltamab versus real-world standard-of-care in triple-class-exposed relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma in the United States

abstract.p: LINKER-MM1 (NCT03761108) is a Phase 1/2 study of linvoseltamab, a human BCMA×CD3 bispecific antibody for patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) who are triple-class exposed (TCE) with ≥3 prior lines of therapy (3L+), or triple-class refractory (TCR). The Phase 2 linvoseltamab 200 mg cohort (N = 105) was compared with an external control arm comprising 149 patients from two US electronic health record databases, COTA and Guardian Research Network, treated with real-world (RW) standard-of-care (SOC). Key LINKER-MM1 eligibility criteria were applied to the RW SOC cohort; an independent data review committee assessed data relevance and quality, and cohort comparability. Inverse probability of treatment weighting was used to balance baseline characteristics between cohorts. The most common SOC regimens were combinations of carfilzomib, pomalidomide, and dexamethasone (8.6%) and daratumumab, pomalidomide, and dexamethasone (8.2%). No patients received chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy or bispecific antibodies. Linvoseltamab had a higher objective response rate than RW SOC (weighted odds ratio 3.8 [95% CI: 2.5–6.6]), and longer median progression-free survival (weighted hazard ratio [wHR] 0.29 [95% CI: 0.23–0.39]), time to next treatment (wHR 0.20 [95% CI: 0.15–0.26]), and overall survival (wHR 0.41 [95% CI: 0.32–0.52]), demonstrating its potential as an effective treatment for 3L+ and TCE/TCR RRMM.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Multiple myeloma (MM) is an incurable malignancy of plasma cells that accounts for 10% of hematologic cancers and 2% of all cancer diagnoses in the United States (US) [1, 2]. The condition affects 7.3 per 100,000 individuals in the US and 1.8 per 100,000 globally. Although current treatments often deliver durable responses, most patients eventually relapse, become refractory, or both, with a median overall survival (OS) of approximately 5.5 years from diagnosis [3–5].

Initial MM treatment typically involves triplet or quadruplet regimens with multiple drug classes such as proteasome inhibitors (PIs), monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs), and corticosteroids. Until recently, patients with relapsed/refractory MM (RRMM) who become triple-class exposed (TCE, i.e., who received prior PI, IMiD, and anti-cluster of differentiation 38 [CD38] mAb therapy) have had relatively limited effective treatment options, particularly among those who are triple-class refractory (TCR). Several promising therapies have recently been approved for TCE/TCR RRMM, including chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapies (first approved in March 2021) [6] and bispecific antibodies (first approved in October 2022) [7], which target the B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) or G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D present on plasma cells. However, although use of these therapies is increasing, most patients still do not receive them [8, 9], and among conventional chemotherapy regimens, both clinical guidelines and actual, real-world (RW) physician’s standard-of-care (SOC) choice in the US (as observed in electronic health records [EHRs]) include a wide variety of regimens [10–13].

Linvoseltamab is a human BCMA×cluster of differentiation 3 (CD3) bispecific antibody that functions by simultaneously engaging plasma cells and T cells, inducing tumor cell lysis [14] and was approved in April 2025 in Europe and July 2025 in the US for the treatment of RRMM [15–17]. The Phase 1/2 LINKER-MM1 clinical trial (NCT03761108) is assessing the efficacy and safety of linvoseltamab in patients with TCE/TCR RRMM who had progressed on their most recent treatment. Results showed that linvoseltamab demonstrated deep and durable responses [18, 19]. The ongoing Phase 2 portion of LINKER-MM1 includes 105 patients receiving the 200 mg linvoseltamab registrational dose [18]. To date, linvoseltamab has not been directly compared with other treatments for TCE/TCR RRMM.

The primary objective of the present study was to assess the distribution of treatments comprised in RW SOC for TCE/TCR RRMM in the US. A secondary objective was to contextualize LINKER-MM1 by comparing objective response rates (ORRs), progression-free survival (PFS), time to next treatment (TTNT), and OS outcomes for patients treated with linvoseltamab with those of patients treated with RW SOC who shared the LINKER-MM1 eligibility criteria.

The present analysis represents the second portion of a two-part study (NCT05673967), in which results from LINKER-MM1 were separately compared against two distinct external control arms (ECAs). The primary ECA cohort, reported elsewhere [20, 21, 22], included patients treated at International Myeloma Foundation International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) sites and therefore reflected the SOC at international academic sites. The secondary ECA cohort, described herein and reported previously [23], included patients from two US EHR sources, COTA and the Guardian Research Network (GRN), and predominantly reflected SOC at US community oncology sites. For each comparison, LINKER-MM1 eligibility criteria were applied to RW data to construct the ECA, and the populations were aligned through inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW).

sec.title: Study Design and Patients
sec.p: The present analysis used de-identified, patient-level data from LINKER-MM1 and two US-based RW EHR sources, COTA and GRN. RW patients with RRMM and ≥3 prior lines of therapy (3L+), TCE or TCR status, and who had initiated MM therapies were identified using structured/unstructured EHR data as available. Patients meeting relevant inclusion and exclusion criteria from LINKER-MM1 (Supplementary Table 1) were included in a pooled, de-duplicated, COTA-GRN RW SOC dataset.

sec.title: LINKER-MM1 trial
sec.p: The linvoseltamab cohort included 105 patients from the Phase 2 LINKER-MM1 trial who received the 200 mg registrational dose at 22 global sites, with 81.0% from the US, 10.5% from Europe, and 8.6% from Asia (data cutoff: July 23, 2024). Additional details on the LINKER-MM1 trial have been published elsewhere [18, 24]. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the International Conference on Harmonization Good Clinical Practice guidelines. The study protocol and all amendments were approved by the institutional review board or independent ethics committee at each participating site and are available online.

sec.title: COTA-GRN RW SOC dataset
sec.p: COTA and GRN data were combined to create an RW SOC cohort as an ECA. COTA is a US-based, longitudinal, oncology EHR database containing detailed clinical, demographic, and outcome data across diverse healthcare settings. It represents RW treatment practices in the US and reflects the distribution of patients with MM nationally, where approximately 80% of patients are treated in community hospitals and 20% in academic centers [25]. COTA captures information on more than 500,000 patients at over 200 sites and has informed previous RW analyses of patients with RRMM [11]. The data abstraction process uses clinical and statistical expertise along with technology to transform structured and unstructured data into a standardized model.

The GRN is a non-profit, cancer-focused, US health system consortium that captures diverse patient data through EHRs, including both structured and unstructured data, such as physician notes and lab results. Clinical professionals review the unstructured data, capturing essential endpoints like disease progression and response rates. GRN data come from community sites only and have also been used in a prior RW RRMM study [11].

Patients in both the COTA and GRN databases were eligible for inclusion in the RW SOC cohort if, after becoming 3L+/TCE or TCR, at least one subsequent line of therapy (LOT) was initiated between November 16, 2015, and December 31, 2021, and they met other key eligibility criteria. Patients could have multiple eligible LOTs. Index dates were defined as the start of each eligible LOT, with the pre-index period covering the time from MM diagnosis up to the day before the index date. The post-index period was defined from day 1 after the index date to the earliest of death, last visit, or end of the study period (June 30, 2022).

sec.title: Eligibility Criteria
sec.p: LINKER-MM1 eligibility criteria were applied to each RW database, COTA, and GRN, separately. Given that not all criteria were applicable to RW clinical practice, the criteria were fully applied or adapted where possible.

Six of 12 inclusion criteria (50%) for the linvoseltamab cohort were applied to the RW SOC cohort, including: age ≥18 years; Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) ≤ 1 at baseline; confirmed MM diagnosis prior to the index date; measurable disease (defined by ≥1 of: serum M-protein ≥1 g/dL, urine M-protein ≥200 mg/24 h, or free light chain levels ≥10 mg/dL); 3L+/TCE or TCR before the index date; and a recorded response of stringent complete response (sCR), complete response (CR), very good partial response (VGPR), partial response (PR), minimal response, stable disease, progressive disease (PD), or death on the LOT being evaluated. Eighteen of 24 exclusion criteria (75%) for the linvoseltamab cohort were applied to the RW SOC cohort, including exclusion for prior treatment with BCMA-directed immunotherapies other than BCMA antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs). Supplementary Table 1 provides further details on the application and/or modification of eligibility criteria.

After applying the eligibility criteria to the COTA and GRN databases separately, they were combined using a prespecified, patient-level tokenization procedure. Patients were linked across datasets using tokenized identifiers without sharing protected information. This resulted in the exclusion of one duplicate patient (with one LOT) from GRN. The two databases were then combined to build the RW SOC cohort, which was compared with patients treated with linvoseltamab.

sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p: Clinical endpoints were assessed as described in Supplementary Table 2 along with the LINKER-MM1 endpoint definitions. ORR was the primary endpoint in the Phase 2 portion of LINKER-MM1 and defined as the proportion of LOTs achieving the best overall response of PR or better. LINKER-MM1 used a blinded independent central review committee for response evaluation, while COTA uses a proprietary algorithm based on the 2016 IMWG criteria [26] that does not include imaging data, and GRN uses physician-documented responses recorded in progress notes.

Additionally, the following secondary endpoints were compared between the linvoseltamab and RW SOC cohorts: PFS, defined as time from study treatment start to first date of PD or death; TTNT, defined as time from study treatment start to subsequent LOT initiation, censoring at death, or data cutoff if no subsequent LOT was received; OS, defined as time from treatment start to death; and duration of response (DOR), which was reported descriptively and defined as time from first documented response (sCR, CR, VGPR, or PR) until PD or death.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: As each RW SOC patient could have contributed multiple eligible LOTs, one LOT per patient was selected. Data with multiple LOTs were first weighted by TCE/TCR status and prior number of LOTs to align with distributions in the linvoseltamab cohort, then one LOT per patient was selected using weighted random sampling prior to IPTW.

After creating the COTA-GRN RW SOC cohort with one LOT per patient, IPTW was used to balance key prognostic factors between the linvoseltamab and RW SOC cohorts. Clinically important prognostic factors were identified through a systematic literature review [27, 28] and were then ranked according to their importance by a panel of five hematology experts [28, 29]. Of the 25 identified factors, 20 were available in both cohorts (Supplementary Table 3). Prognostic factors were selected for adjustment based on availability in both cohorts, having <30% missingness, and meeting prespecified criteria of effective sample size (ESS) ≥100 and ESS per degree of freedom ≥10 after running IPTW. The following key prognostic factors were included in IPTW: cytogenetic risk, age at index date, TCR status, ECOG PS, platelet count, and sex. Adjustment for these factors started with the first five ranked factors, as prespecified, with additional factors sequentially included based on rank if ESS and ESS per degree of freedom criteria were met. Only sex, the lowest-ranked additional covariate, satisfied these criteria and was included. Per protocol, baseline factors with <30% missingness were imputed via multiple imputation by chained equations [30], although ECOG PS was included regardless of the proportion of missing information. Weights obtained from IPTW were stabilized to target the average treatment effect on the treated, with weights truncated at 4. Balance in prognostic factors across cohorts was evaluated using standardized mean differences (SMDs), with absolute SMDs (aSMDs) ≤0.1 considered well-balanced, >0.1 and ≤0.2 moderately balanced, and >0.2 unbalanced.

For ORR comparisons between the two cohorts, a weighted logistic regression model was used. The reverse Kaplan–Meier (KM) method was used for the computation of median (range) duration of follow-up per endpoint in the unweighted RW SOC cohort. PFS, TTNT, and OS were compared using the weighted KM estimator and weighted Cox proportional hazard models. Unweighted and weighted odds ratios (ORs) for ORR, as well as hazard ratios (HRs) for PFS, TTNT, and OS, were reported. Bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrapping with 500 iterations was used to construct 95% confidence intervals (CIs). P-values were obtained using the ratio of the point estimates to the standard error derived from the 95% CI limits [31]. To address multiplicity in testing the primary and secondary endpoints, a fixed-sequence procedure was conducted (α = 0.05), starting with the primary endpoint (ORR) followed by secondary endpoints in a predefined order: PFS, TTNT, and OS. DOR was analyzed descriptively. All analyses were performed in R (version 4.3.2).

sec.title: Sensitivity Analyses
sec.p: Several sensitivity analyses were conducted to explore alternate definitions of some outcomes, which were assessed differently in the LINKER-MM1 trial compared with the RW data, and to address missing RW data, such as life expectancy assessments. The primary analysis of ORR was repeated with a more stringent definition of best overall response ≥VGPR rather than ≥PR as in the primary analysis. Next, ORR was assessed to include non-evaluable responses as non-response as opposed to non-evaluable responses being excluded from the primary analysis. In addition, time-to-event outcomes used alternative definitions: PFS was analyzed by treating the start of a new LOT after the index date as a PD event rather than a censoring criterion, as in the primary analysis, and TTNT was analyzed by treating death as an event rather than a censoring criterion, as in the primary analysis. All outcomes were also re-assessed using a life expectancy prediction model, with patients who had a predicted life expectancy of <6 months excluded. E-values for each comparative endpoint were reported, which indicated the strength of the relationship an unmeasured confounder would need to have with both the treatment and outcome to nullify any observed effect estimates [32]. Finally, to address potential temporal confounding, a sensitivity analysis was conducted in which the RW SOC cohort was partitioned by calendar era of index-therapy initiation relative to the LINKER-MM1 accrual window. The linvoseltamab cohort was compared with RW SOC patients initiating during the LINKER-MM1 accrual period (“overlap era”) and with those initiating before that period (“non-overlap era”).

sec.title: Subgroup Analyses
sec.p: Analyses of ORR, PFS, TTNT, and OS were performed within levels of top-ranked covariates with a minimum weighted sample size ≥10. This included age groups (<65 years, 65–74 years, ≥75 years), ECOG PS (0 or 1), cytogenetic risk (high or standard), International Staging System stage, presence of extramedullary plasmacytomas, and refractory status (triple-class, quadruple-drug, or penta-drug refractory).

sec.title: Independent Data Review Committee
sec.p: A five-member independent data review committee (IDRC) was convened to review the relevance and quality of data, and the comparability of populations prior to a formal comparison between the linvoseltamab cohort and the RW SOC cohort. The IDRC included two MM experts, two clinical epidemiologists, and one health decision scientist who assessed data relevance, quality, and completeness. The IDRC assessed all data sources, procedures, methodologies, and cohort comparability, although blinded to outcome data, and provided recommendations to enhance robustness and validity of the analyses, which were implemented prior to it formally endorsing the comparative analysis [33].

sec.title: Population
sec.p: The linvoseltamab cohort included 105 patients (one LOT per patient) with 3L+/TCE or TCR RRMM. In the COTA database, 90 patients (133 eligible LOTs) out of 2352 patients with MM met all applicable eligibility criteria. In the GRN database, 60 patients (88 eligible LOTs) out of 344 patients with MM met all applicable eligibility criteria. The eligible data from COTA and GRN were combined, resulting in 150 patients (221 eligible LOTs). After de-duplication, one duplicate patient (with one LOT) was identified and retained in COTA due to more complete information, although removed from GRN. The final COTA-GRN RW SOC dataset included 149 unique patients (220 eligible LOTs), of whom 36% received treatment in academic centers, and 64% were treated in community hospitals. Details are provided in Supplementary Tables 4 and 5.

sec.title: Baseline Characteristics
sec.p:
Baseline characteristics are presented in Table 1 for the linvoseltamab and RW SOC cohorts. The linvoseltamab cohort had a higher proportion of patients with high cytogenetic risk, TCR status, and ECOG PS of 1, whereas the RW SOC cohort had a higher proportion of patients receiving prior hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) and longer time to relapse from HSCT. sec.title: Distribution of Treatment Regimens in the RW SOC Cohort
sec.p:
Treatments observed in the RW SOC cohort are reported in Supplementary Table 6, including 87 unique regimens across 146 LOTs. The most common regimens in the weighted cohort included: carfilzomib, pomalidomide, and dexamethasone (8.6%); daratumumab, pomalidomide, and dexamethasone (8.2%); and any anti-CD38 mAb, carfilzomib, and dexamethasone (4.5%); with 1.3% receiving an ADC, and none receiving CAR-T therapies or bispecific antibodies. In addition, the distribution of the categorized treatment regimens across index LOTs is presented in Table 2. The most frequently reported categorized treatment regimen in the weighted RW SOC cohort included PI + IMiD (15.6%), anti-CD38 + IMiD (12.0%), multi-drug chemotherapy regimens containing cyclophosphamide and etoposide and/or doxorubicin (8.6%), PI (8.0%), and PI + alkylating agent (7.6%).Table 2

sec.title: Objective Response Rate
sec.p:
In the primary analysis excluding non-evaluable responses, the ORR was higher in patients in the linvoseltamab cohort (69.5%) compared with the weighted RW SOC cohort (37.3%), resulting in a weighted OR of 3.8 (95% CI: 2.5–6.6; p < 0.001; Table 3). The E-value for this OR was 3.3 with a CI lower bound of 2.5, indicating that any unmeasured confounder would need to have an association with both ORR and treatment of at least 2.5 (expressed as a risk ratio) to potentially negate the observed effect for ORR (Supplementary Table 7). Sensitivity analyses accounting for non-evaluable responses in the RW SOC cohort by treating them as non-responses (Supplementary Table 8) resulted in a lower ORR, and those that excluded patients with life expectancies of <6 months (Supplementary Table 9) resulted in an ORR consistent with the primary analysis. Notably, patients in the linvoseltamab cohort were markedly more likely to have a best overall response of ≥VGPR compared with the weighted RW SOC cohort (62.9% vs. 5.4%, respectively), yielding a weighted OR of 29.4 (95% CI: 13.0–103.2; p < 0.001; Supplementary Table 10). Results remained consistent with the primary analysis when linvoseltamab was compared with RW SOC in the overlap (OR 2.8, 95% CI: 1.1–7.1) and non-overlap (OR 4.2, 95% CI: 2.3–7.7) eras (Supplementary Table 11).Table 3

sec.title: Time to Next Treatment
sec.p: The median TTNT was not reached in the linvoseltamab cohort compared with 6.6 months in the weighted RW SOC cohort, resulting in a weighted HR of 0.20 (95% CI: 0.15–0.26; p < 0.001) (Table 4, Fig. 1B). For this HR, the E-value and its CI upper bound were 5.4 and 4.4, respectively (Supplementary Table 7). Sensitivity analyses showed consistent results when linvoseltamab was compared with the overlap and non-overlap eras (Supplementary Table 11), when death was defined as a TTNT event rather than a censoring criterion (Supplementary Table 12), and when excluding patients predicted to have life expectancies of <6 months (Supplementary Table 13).

sec.title: Overall Survival
sec.p: The median OS was 27.8 months in the linvoseltamab cohort compared with 10.1 months in the weighted RW SOC cohort, yielding a weighted HR of 0.41 (95% CI: 0.32–0.52; p < 0.001; Table 4, Fig. 1C). For this HR, the E-value and its CI upper bound were 3.1 and 2.5, respectively (Supplementary Table 7). Results from the sensitivity analysis comparing linvoseltamab with the overlap and non-overlap eras (Supplementary Table 11) were consistent with the primary analysis. Median OS was consistent with the main OS results when excluding patients predicted to have life expectancies of <6 months (Supplementary Table 13).

sec.title: Duration of Response
sec.p: The median DOR was not reached in the linvoseltamab cohort compared with 6.6 months in the weighted RW SOC cohort (Table 4, Fig. 1D). Median DOR was consistent with the main DOR results when separating the RW SOC cohort into overlap and non-overlap eras (Supplementary Table 11) and when excluding patients predicted to have life expectancies of <6 months (Supplementary Table 13).

sec.title: Subgroup Analyses
sec.p: Results of predefined subgroup analyses were generally consistent with the primary analyses, favoring linvoseltamab in all cases. However, for some subgroups, notably International Staging System stage and presence of extramedullary plasmacytomas, low sample sizes in the ECA led to wide CIs (Supplementary Fig. 2).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Results from this study show that linvoseltamab achieved significantly higher ORR and prolonged OS, PFS, and TTNT compared with COTA-GRN RW SOC therapy in patients with TCE RRMM. Eighty-seven unique regimens were reported in the RW SOC cohort across the combined COTA-GRN database, broadly reflecting the TCE RRMM treatment landscape in the US and demonstrating the lack of SOC in RRMM [11–13]. RW patients largely received conventional regimens delivered in community settings, and few received recently approved therapies.

Great care was taken to approximate clinical trial conditions for the ECA as closely as possible to ensure robust comparisons. Relevant prognostic factors were determined objectively using a systematic literature review, then supplemented and ranked as per expert opinion. Similarly, the use of an IDRC, which assessed the comparability of the two cohorts and evaluated all methodological approaches and decisions before endorsing proceeding to a formal comparison, enhanced the scientific rigor of the study. Eligibility criteria from the clinical trial were also screened and applied to the RW data to a greater extent than in earlier published trials, using EHR sources such as COTA or Flatiron [26, 34–36], allowing for robust comparisons between the clinical trial and ECA. In addition, E-values were generated for all comparative estimates to determine the strength of the association an unidentified confounder would need to have to negate the observed effect size. In all cases, this would have required an unobserved treatment effect with a risk ratio of at least 2.5, which is unlikely given the degree of expert involvement to identify strong prognostic factors a priori.

An expansive set of sensitivity analyses was also performed to ensure robustness of results to assumptions, including imputing missing response data as non-response, assessing PFS with initiation of a new LOT considered a progression event, and with TTNT assessed with death considered an event alongside initiation of a new LOT. In all cases, the results of these sensitivity analyses were consistent with or more favorable for linvoseltamab compared with those of the main analyses, highlighting the robustness of the results. In addition, a model predicting life expectancy was used to exclude RW SOC patients who would have likely been excluded from LINKER-MM1 based on physicians’ baseline life expectancy estimates, better aligning the ECA with the clinical trial cohort and improving comparability in the face of missing data. One final sensitivity analysis increased the threshold for objective response to best overall response ≥VGPR rather than ≥PR, with stronger results for linvoseltamab compared with RW SOC. This highlights that the depth of response was greater in the linvoseltamab cohort, where 66/105 patients (62.9%) reached ≥VGPR, including 54/105 achieving ≥CR and 46/105 with a sCR. This stands in contrast to the response in the RW SOC cohort, which was overwhelmingly driven by PR alone (37/113). Only 9 of 113 patients (8.0%) with evaluable responses achieved ≥VGPR of whom only 1/113 achieved a CR. However, this may potentially underestimate the true rate due to infrequent efficacy evaluation in the community.

Response assessments were made differently between cohorts. The linvoseltamab cohort was subject to an independent central review committee to determine response based on IMWG criteria. In contrast, COTA applied a proprietary algorithm that was based on the same 2016 IMWG criteria, and GRN reported physician-assessed responses from progress notes [37]. Importantly, LINKER-MM1 patients received treatment at academic sites, whereas COTA-GRN RW SOC patients were largely treated at community sites, where SOC may differ based on access to the newest therapies and clinical expertise. An additional limitation is residual confounding and an imbalance between cohorts in some of the key prognostic factors, most notably the number of prior LOTs, prior HSCT, and time to relapse from HSCT, with higher values for all in the RW SOC cohort than in the linvoseltamab cohort. This may negatively affect results for RW SOC, given the greater burden of illness; however, as noted previously, any meaningful imbalances would need to generate large treatment effects exceeding the minimum E-values calculated to negate the observed treatment benefits of linvoseltamab.

ECAs in RRMM have previously leveraged databases similar to those described here [34–36, 38], as well as prospective RW SOC studies such as LocoMMotion and MoMMent [12, 39–41], and have included patients from both community and academic sites. Results across these ECAs, including those comparing bispecific therapies such as teclistamab [40], elranatamab [34], and talquetamab [38, 41] with RW cohorts, were largely consistent with the study results reported here for linvoseltamab. The ORR ranged from 26% to 32% in historical ECAs and other RW sources [11, 12, 34, 40–43] compared with 37.3% (when excluding non-evaluable responses) and 28.7% (when treating non-evaluable responses as non-response) in this ECA, although linvoseltamab-treated patients achieved an ORR of 69.5% in LINKER-MM1. Median PFS was also similar across RW sources, ranging from 3.4 to 4.6 months in historical data [11, 12, 34, 35, 38, 40–43] compared with 3.9 months in this ECA, and was not reached for linvoseltamab in LINKER-MM1. Similarly, median OS ranged from 9.2 months to 16.5 months in historical RW sources [11, 12, 34, 35, 38, 40–43] compared with 10.1 months in this ECA, and was 27.8 months for linvoseltamab in LINKER-MM1.

The similarity of outcomes between ECAs is not surprising, given their use of similar study designs and enrollment of similar US and EU patients in overlapping periods. Furthermore, all had negligible levels of recently approved therapies for patients with TCE/TCR disease (which might otherwise drive differences), such as CAR-T (0% in this ECA vs. 0–1.7% in published ECAs), anti-BCMA ADCs (1.3% in this ECA vs. 0–5.6% in historical ECAs), and anti-BCMA bispecific antibodies (none in either cohort) [34, 35, 40, 41]. The low rates likely reflect a lack of access due to the recency of approvals, and that community sites would be unlikely to have access to experimental therapies [44]. Additionally, recent studies conducted to assess CAR-T therapy access have found that patients often have to overcome many barriers, and in the US, this disproportionately affects Black patients [45–47]. While access to CAR-T therapies is likely to increase in future ECAs, easier-to-administer drugs like bispecifics can also help improve access to the best treatments for patients who cannot get care in the most advanced treatment centers. This effect can already be seen in practice as patient outcomes continue to improve with the introduction of mAbs, bispecific antibodies, anti-BMCA ADCs, and CAR-T therapies. Hence, as expected, patient outcomes in the primary ECA cohort were found to be better compared with patient outcomes in past ECAs [22]. However, in spite of the similarities, it should be noted there are some important methodological differences relative to previous ECAs, such as the application of more extensive eligibility criteria from the relevant clinical trial, a prespecified covariate list based on a systematic literature review and physician review panel, as well as the outcome-blinded review of the quality and relevance of all data sources, procedures and methods, and cohort comparability by the IDRC.

At the time this study was conducted, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network-preferred treatments for patients with TCE/TCR disease included the CAR-T therapies idecabtagene vicleucel (ide-cel) and ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) for those exposed to 3 prior LOTs [10, 48]. Since completion of this study, National Comprehensive Cancer Network recommendations have expanded for ide-cel to include TCE patients with 2 prior LOTs, and for cilta-cel to patients with 1 prior LOT, including an IMiD and PI, who are refractory to lenalidomide. Bispecific antibodies such as linvoseltamab, teclistamab, elranatamab, and talquetamab are recommended for those exposed to 4 LOTs, and the ADC belantamab mafodotin is now considered useful only in certain circumstances [10]. Given the low utilization of these therapies observed in this study and in other historical ECAs, they better reflect the conventional SOC regimens used in community hospitals rather than academic centers during the study period. Community hospitals may have had less access to novel therapies or lacked the required interdisciplinary expertise and/or support staff to administer them [44], and substantially longer OS has previously been shown in patients with MM when treated at US academic sites compared with community sites [49].

The results of this study largely reflect a US patient population (89.7% in the linvoseltamab cohort and 100% in the RW SOC cohort), with 64% of RW patients treated at community sites and 36% treated at academic sites. The low prevalence of academic-site treatment in the ECA and its corresponding impact on treatments represented may have a substantial impact on the observed outcomes. In contrast to the secondary ECA cohort from NCT05673967 described here, the primary ECA cohort (described elsewhere) [20, 21, 22] included patients treated exclusively at academic International Myeloma Foundation IMWG centers, and showed substantially better outcomes than those reported in the COTA-GRN RW SOC here; however, in both analyses, linvoseltamab was more effective than RW SOC.

In conclusion, findings from this study demonstrated significantly improved efficacy with linvoseltamab treatment compared with RW SOC across community oncology sites in the US. Results were consistent across all study endpoints and both sensitivity and subgroup analyses. Overall, they suggest that linvoseltamab provides an effective and promising treatment option for patients with RRMM.
